# Sacubitril/Valsartan in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and hospitalization worldwide, affecting more than 60 million people [1]. For decades, neurohormonal blockade with renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors and beta-blockers formed the cornerstone of therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [2]. The introduction of sacubitril/valsartan, the first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), represented a paradigm shift in pharmacotherapy [3].

## Mechanism of Action

Sacubitril/valsartan combines the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril with the angiotensin receptor blocker valsartan in a single supramolecular complex [4]. Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase that degrades several vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [5]. By inhibiting neprilysin, the drug augments natriuretic peptide activity, promoting natriuresis, diuresis, vasodilation, and inhibition of pathological cardiac remodeling [6]. Because neprilysin inhibition alone raises angiotensin II levels, concurrent angiotensin receptor blockade with valsartan is essential to achieve net benefit [7]. The combination of neprilysin inhibition with ACE inhibition was abandoned in earlier trials (omapatrilat) owing to an unacceptable risk of angioedema, prompting the strategic pairing with an ARB instead [8].

## Pivotal Clinical Trial Evidence

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial randomized 8442 patients with HFrEF (NYHA class II–IV, ejection fraction ≤40%, later ≤35%) to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril [3]. The trial was stopped early for overwhelming benefit: sacubitril/valsartan reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20%, and reduced all-cause mortality significantly compared with enalapril [3,9]. The benefit was consistent across prespecified subgroups [10]. Sacubitril/valsartan also reduced sudden cardiac death and improved symptoms and quality of life [11,12]. Analyses demonstrated reductions in NT-proBNP and troponin, reflecting decreased myocardial wall stress and injury [13].

In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the PARAGON-HF trial randomized 4822 patients with ejection fraction ≥45% to sacubitril/valsartan versus valsartan [14]. The primary composite of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death narrowly missed statistical significance (rate ratio 0.87, p=0.06) [14]. However, subgroup analyses suggested benefit in patients with lower ejection fractions and in women [15,16]. A pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF supported a therapeutic effect that diminishes with increasing ejection fraction [17].

The PIONEER-HF trial demonstrated that in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan among patients stabilized after acute decompensated HF was safe and produced greater NT-proBNP reduction than enalapril [18]. The TRANSITION trial similarly confirmed feasibility of early in-hospital or post-discharge initiation [19]. The PROVE-HF study linked sacubitril/valsartan therapy to reverse cardiac remodeling, with reductions in left ventricular volumes and improvements in ejection fraction [20].

## Guideline Recommendations and Clinical Use

Contemporary guidelines from the ACC/AHA/HFSA and the European Society of Cardiology recommend ARNI as a foundational therapy for HFrEF, often as a replacement for ACE inhibitors or ARBs [21,22]. Sacubitril/valsartan is now considered one of the four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy alongside beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors [23]. Some experts advocate early simultaneous or rapid sequential initiation of all four agents to maximize survival benefit [24].

## Safety and Tolerability

The most important adverse effects include symptomatic hypotension, hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction, and angioedema [3,25]. A 36-hour washout period is required when switching from an ACE inhibitor to avoid overlapping neprilysin and ACE inhibition that increases angioedema risk [21]. Theoretical concerns that neprilysin inhibition might impair amyloid-beta clearance and affect cognition prompted the PERSPECTIVE trial, which did not demonstrate significant cognitive harm [26]. Hyperkalemia rates were comparable to or lower than ACE inhibitor comparators [27].

## Cost-Effectiveness and Implementation

Despite robust evidence, uptake of sacubitril/valsartan has been variable owing to cost, clinical inertia, and tolerability concerns [28]. Cost-effectiveness analyses generally find the therapy to fall within accepted willingness-to-pay thresholds in high-income settings [29]. Real-world registries confirm benefits consistent with randomized trials, though up-titration to target doses remains suboptimal in clinical practice [30].

## Conclusion

Sacubitril/valsartan has transformed the management of HFrEF, delivering substantial reductions in mortality and hospitalization beyond conventional RAS inhibition [3,9]. Its role in HFpEF is more nuanced, with possible benefit at the lower end of the preserved ejection fraction spectrum [14,17]. As a pillar of modern guideline-directed therapy, ongoing efforts should focus on early initiation, dose optimization, and equitable implementation to maximize population-level outcomes [23,24].
